title: SGLT2 Inhibitors: Ketoacidosis, Volume, and Genitourinary Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin increase urinary glucose excretion and may provide glucose, heart-failure, and kidney benefits in selected patients. Major nursing safety issues are volume depletion, genitourinary infection, and ketoacidosis that can occur with glucose lower than expected.
recognize: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, dyspnea, or confusion can signal ketoacidosis even without marked hyperglycemia.
Genital mycotic infections and urinary infections occur more often because of glycosuria.
priorities: Assess hydration, renal function, infection symptoms, and ketoacidosis symptoms before routine continuation during acute illness.
Follow the prescribed temporary-hold plan around surgery, prolonged fasting, or severe acute illness.
Escalate suspected ketoacidosis and obtain ketone/acid-base evaluation as ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, renal function, volume status, BP, genital/urinary symptoms, and ketones when clinically indicated.
interventions: Promote appropriate hydration and genital hygiene while avoiding unnecessary fluid loading in heart/kidney failure.
medicationSafety: Risk of ketoacidosis rises with fasting, acute illness, reduced insulin, surgery, and heavy alcohol use.
Older adults and patients on diuretics may be more susceptible to volume depletion.
redFlags: Severe perineal pain/swelling with systemic illness
teaching: Know the sick-day and surgery hold plan, maintain hydration as directed, and seek care for ketoacidosis symptoms even if glucose is not extremely high.
delegationScope: Routine glucose collection may be delegated where allowed; suspected ketoacidosis or severe infection requires licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Ruling out SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis because the glucose is not dramatically elevated.
oneLinePearl: SGLT2 ketoacidosis can be relatively euglycemic—symptoms matter more than one glucose number.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care 2026

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: GI Effects, Gallbladder, and Pancreas
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide slow gastric emptying, increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, reduce glucagon, and often reduce appetite. Common GI effects can become clinically important when persistent vomiting causes dehydration; severe persistent abdominal pain raises concern for pancreatitis or gallbladder disease.
recognize: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, early satiety, and reduced appetite are common, especially during dose escalation.
Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, persistent vomiting, or RUQ pain/fever requires evaluation.
priorities: Assess hydration, GI tolerance, glucose response, renal function during major GI losses, and abdominal red flags.
Verify the exact product and dose because formulations/indications differ.
Review personal/family medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 history when relevant to the specific labeled product.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, glucose/A1C, GI symptoms, hydration, renal function during dehydration, and signs of gallbladder/pancreatic disease.
interventions: Encourage smaller meals and adequate fluids as tolerated during mild GI effects; escalate persistent vomiting or inability to maintain intake.
medicationSafety: When combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, hypoglycemia risk can increase even though GLP-1 drugs alone have low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk.
Delayed gastric emptying can affect oral-drug absorption and peri-procedural aspiration planning; follow current anesthesia/procedural instructions.
complications: Aspiration risk in selected procedural settings
teaching: Use the exact injection schedule/product instructions, do not double missed doses outside the product plan, and report severe persistent abdominal pain or vomiting.
delegationScope: Persistent GI losses, pancreatitis/gallbladder symptoms, or significant hypoglycemia require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming all nausea on a GLP-1 drug is harmless even when the patient cannot keep fluids down and has severe abdominal pain.
oneLinePearl: GLP-1 drugs slow the gut—watch hydration and severe abdominal pain.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care 2026

title: Glucagon: Severe Hypoglycemia Rescue
bottomLine: Glucagon is an emergency treatment for severe hypoglycemia when the patient cannot safely take oral carbohydrate and IV dextrose is not immediately available or appropriate. Recovery must be followed by reassessment, carbohydrate intake when safe, and investigation of the cause because hypoglycemia can recur.
recognize: Seizure, unconsciousness, severe confusion, or inability to swallow safely makes oral glucose unsafe.
Glucagon can cause nausea/vomiting, so aspiration precautions matter during recovery.
priorities: Protect airway and position side-lying when possible because vomiting may occur.
Administer the available glucagon product according to its device instructions/protocol.
Recheck glucose and neurologic status and activate emergency care for severe or persistent hypoglycemia.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, consciousness, airway/swallowing, recent insulin/sulfonylurea exposure, food intake, renal function, alcohol use, and recurrence.
interventions: Once awake and safe to swallow, provide fast carbohydrate followed by a longer-acting source according to the care plan.
medicationSafety: Glucagon relies partly on hepatic glycogen stores and may be less effective after prolonged fasting, severe malnutrition, or substantial alcohol-related glycogen depletion.
Sulfonylurea-associated hypoglycemia can recur after initial rescue.
teaching: Family/caregivers should know where rescue glucagon is stored, how the specific device works, and to call emergency services after severe episodes according to the emergency plan.
delegationScope: Emergency glucagon use may be protocol/delegation dependent by setting; licensed nursing assessment is required after severe hypoglycemia.
examTrap: Giving juice to an unconscious hypoglycemic patient instead of using a non-oral rescue pathway.
oneLinePearl: Unsafe swallow means no oral glucose—use rescue treatment and protect the airway.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care 2026

title: Thiazide Diuretics: Sodium, Potassium, Glucose, and Gout
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Thiazide-type diuretics are common antihypertensives that can cause hyponatremia, hypokalemia, volume depletion, hyperuricemia, and glucose changes. Older adults are especially vulnerable to falls and confusion from sodium or volume loss.
recognize: Weakness, cramps, palpitations, dizziness, falls, or confusion can reflect electrolyte or volume disturbance.
Acute painful swollen joint may reflect gout in a susceptible patient.
priorities: Assess BP/orthostasis, electrolytes, renal function, hydration, and gout/diabetes history.
Schedule administration to reduce nocturia when clinically appropriate.
Escalate symptomatic hyponatremia, severe hypokalemia, or syncope.
assessMonitor: Trend sodium, potassium, creatinine, BP, weight when indicated, glucose, uric acid when clinically relevant, and falls.
interventions: Use fall precautions during initiation/titration and reinforce ordered potassium/diet plans rather than assuming supplementation is always needed.
medicationSafety: Hyponatremia can be severe, especially in older adults.
Lithium concentrations can rise when thiazides reduce renal lithium clearance.
redFlags: Lithium toxicity symptoms after starting a thiazide
teaching: Change positions slowly, monitor BP as instructed, and report severe weakness, confusion, fainting, or gout symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine BP/weights may be delegated with thresholds; electrolyte-related symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Starting a thiazide in a patient taking lithium without recognizing the interaction risk.
oneLinePearl: Thiazides lower pressure but can also lower sodium and potassium—and raise lithium and uric acid.

title: Diltiazem and Verapamil: AV Node, Pressure, and Heart Failure
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers slow AV-node conduction and reduce heart rate while lowering blood pressure. Monitor for bradycardia, heart block, hypotension, constipation (especially verapamil), and worsening systolic heart failure in susceptible patients.
recognize: Dizziness, fatigue, bradycardia, edema, and constipation may occur.
Combination with beta blockers or digoxin can intensify AV-node slowing.
priorities: Check HR/rhythm, BP, symptoms, and ordered hold parameters.
Assess for new heart-failure symptoms before continuing when clinically indicated.
Escalate symptomatic bradycardia, hypotension, or high-grade block.
assessMonitor: Trend HR/rhythm, BP, edema/weight, dyspnea, constipation, and interacting AV-node drugs.
interventions: Use fall precautions for orthostasis and bowel-regimen support when ordered for constipation.
medicationSafety: Avoid or use cautiously in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure according to the treatment plan because negative inotropy can worsen decompensation.
Do not combine multiple AV-node blockers casually; review the medication plan.
teaching: Check pulse/BP if instructed, report fainting or worsening dyspnea/edema, and prevent constipation as directed.
delegationScope: IV titration/rhythm management depends on state/facility competency; acute rhythm or perfusion changes require licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Giving an AV-node blocker to a patient with marked symptomatic bradycardia without checking the order parameters and rhythm.
oneLinePearl: Diltiazem/verapamil slow the AV node—watch rate, pressure, and pump function.

title: Ipratropium and Tiotropium: Anticholinergic Bronchodilation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilators reduce vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. Ipratropium is short-acting and often used in COPD exacerbation regimens; tiotropium is long-acting maintenance therapy and is not a rescue medication for acute bronchospasm.
recognize: Dry mouth and throat irritation are common.
Anticholinergic effects can worsen urinary retention or precipitate narrow-angle glaucoma symptoms if aerosol contacts the eyes in susceptible patients.
priorities: Verify whether the medication is rescue/short-acting or maintenance/long-acting.
Assess breath sounds, work of breathing, inhaler technique, urinary symptoms, and eye complaints.
Use a true rescue bronchodilator for acute bronchospasm according to the action plan.
assessMonitor: Trend dyspnea, rescue-inhaler use, urinary retention, dry mouth, eye pain/blurred vision, and technique.
interventions: Teach correct inhaler/nebulizer technique and avoid spraying medication into the eyes.
medicationSafety: Tiotropium and other long-acting anticholinergics do not replace rapid rescue therapy during an acute attack.
Use caution in urinary retention/BPH and narrow-angle glaucoma.
complications: Treatment delay if mistaken for rescue medication
teaching: Know which inhaler is rescue and which is maintenance; use device-specific technique and report urinary retention or acute eye symptoms.
delegationScope: Inhaler reinforcement can be delegated after education, but acute respiratory deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Using tiotropium as the first rescue drug during severe acute bronchospasm.

title: Montelukast: Maintenance Drug With Neuropsychiatric Warning
bottomLine: Montelukast is a leukotriene-receptor antagonist used for chronic asthma prevention, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction prevention, and selected allergic-rhinitis patients; it does not treat an acute asthma attack. Serious neuropsychiatric events carry a boxed warning and require prompt action.
recognize: Agitation, aggression, sleep disturbance, depression, abnormal dreams, suicidal thoughts/behavior, or other behavioral changes can occur.
For allergic rhinitis, use is generally reserved for patients who do not respond to or tolerate alternatives because of the neuropsychiatric risk.
priorities: Assess baseline mental-health history and new behavior/mood changes.
Confirm the patient still has an acute rescue inhaler/action plan for asthma.
Discontinue and contact the prescriber promptly if new neuropsychiatric symptoms occur according to labeling guidance.
assessMonitor: Trend asthma control, rescue use, exercise symptoms, mood, sleep, behavior, and suicidal thinking.
interventions: Reinforce controller adherence and environmental/allergy strategies as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Montelukast is not a bronchodilator and cannot replace albuterol during an acute attack.
Chewable products may contain phenylalanine; check formulation for patients with phenylketonuria.
complications: Poor asthma control if used as rescue therapy
redFlags: Acute asthma distress not responding to rescue therapy
teaching: Report new mood, sleep, or behavioral changes immediately and keep the prescribed rescue inhaler available for acute symptoms.
delegationScope: Behavioral changes and acute asthma deterioration require licensed-nurse assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Giving montelukast for immediate relief of an acute asthma attack.
oneLinePearl: Montelukast prevents; it does not rescue—and mood changes matter.

title: Theophylline: Narrow Therapeutic Window and Major Interactions
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and many illness, smoking, and drug interactions that change clearance. Repetitive nausea/vomiting, tremor, severe restlessness, tachyarrhythmia, or seizure should be treated as possible toxicity and additional doses withheld pending urgent evaluation.
recognize: Early toxicity often causes nausea, vomiting, insomnia, tremor, or tachycardia; severe toxicity can cause refractory dysrhythmias and seizures.
Fever, heart failure, liver disease, older age, sepsis/shock, and stopping smoking can reduce clearance.
priorities: Review serum concentration when ordered, interacting medications, smoking-status changes, fever/acute illness, and liver/cardiac disease.
Withhold and escalate when toxicity symptoms occur.
Do not increase theophylline simply because acute respiratory symptoms worsened without checking level/context.
assessMonitor: Trend heart rate/rhythm, neurologic symptoms, GI symptoms, serum concentration, smoking status, fever, and interacting drugs.
interventions: Keep extended-release dosing and food timing consistent according to the product instructions; do not crush extended-release tablets.
medicationSafety: Macrolides and other metabolism inhibitors can raise concentrations; enzyme inducers can lower them.
Cessation of cigarette smoking can significantly reduce clearance and raise levels.
teaching: Report vomiting, racing heartbeat, severe tremor, or seizure symptoms and tell the care team if smoking habits or interacting medications change.
delegationScope: Toxicity symptoms and serum-level interpretation require licensed-nurse/provider escalation.
examTrap: Increasing a theophylline dose during an acute exacerbation without checking toxicity risk or serum concentration.
oneLinePearl: Theophylline levels change when illness, smoking, or interacting drugs change.

title: Clozapine: ANC Monitoring, Infection, Myocarditis, and Constipation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Clozapine is highly effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and recurrent suicidal behavior in selected patients but can cause severe neutropenia, myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, seizures, orthostatic hypotension, and dangerous GI hypomotility. The U.S. Clozapine REMS was removed in 2025, but ANC monitoring remains recommended.
recognize: Fever, sore throat, oral ulcers, or infection can signal neutropenia.
Chest pain, dyspnea, persistent tachycardia, fever, or unexplained fatigue early in therapy can signal myocarditis.
Constipation can progress to ileus/obstruction and should not be minimized.
priorities: Verify required ANC monitoring and assess infection symptoms.
Ask actively about bowel movements and GI symptoms.
Escalate myocarditis symptoms, severe constipation/abdominal distention, syncope, or seizure.
assessMonitor: Trend ANC per current prescribing information, orthostatic BP, pulse, bowel function, weight/metabolic measures, seizure symptoms, and myocarditis/cardiomyopathy signs.
interventions: Use a proactive bowel regimen when prescribed and fall precautions during titration.
medicationSafety: FDA removed the mandatory REMS program effective June 13, 2025; do not teach obsolete REMS enrollment requirements.
ANC surveillance remains clinically important because severe neutropenia risk persists.
Abrupt interruption may require re-titration because orthostatic/cardiac risks are dose-titration dependent.
redFlags: Fever/sore throat with low ANC concern
No bowel movement with severe distention/vomiting
teaching: Keep ANC monitoring appointments, report infection or cardiac symptoms promptly, and report constipation early rather than waiting for severe abdominal symptoms.
delegationScope: ANC interpretation, restart/titration decisions, and severe adverse-effect assessment require authorized clinician review.
examTrap: Teaching that clozapine can only be dispensed through the REMS program after FDA removed that requirement in 2025.
oneLinePearl: Clozapine: ANC still matters even though the REMS no longer does.
sourceBasis: FDA 2025 Clozapine REMS Removal Drug Safety Communication

title: Tricyclic Antidepressants: Anticholinergic Effects and Lethal Overdose Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Tricyclic antidepressants can cause sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac conduction toxicity. Overdose can be rapidly fatal from sodium-channel blockade, dysrhythmia, hypotension, and seizure, so medication quantity and suicide risk matter.
recognize: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, sedation, and orthostasis are common anticholinergic effects.
Overdose may present with altered mental status, wide-QRS dysrhythmia, hypotension, seizures, or anticholinergic toxicity.
priorities: Assess suicide/overdose risk, falls, urinary retention, constipation, glaucoma risk, and cardiac disease.
Escalate suspected overdose immediately with continuous ECG and emergency toxicology care.
Use careful titration and fall precautions in older adults.
assessMonitor: Trend mood/suicidality, BP/orthostasis, bowel/bladder function, sedation, ECG when indicated, and interacting serotonergic/anticholinergic drugs.
interventions: Support hydration/fiber/bowel plan when safe and use oral-care measures for dry mouth.
medicationSafety: TCAs can be dangerous in overdose; sodium bicarbonate is a key emergency treatment for significant cardiac sodium-channel blockade under toxicology/emergency protocols.
Concurrent MAOIs or other serotonergic drugs can cause serious interactions.
teaching: Take only as prescribed, avoid unapproved sedating/anticholinergic drugs, and seek emergency help for overdose.
delegationScope: Overdose or severe anticholinergic/cardiac findings require immediate licensed-nurse/emergency escalation.
examTrap: Assuming an antidepressant overdose is low risk because the medication is not an opioid or benzodiazepine.
oneLinePearl: TCA overdose kills through the heart and brain—treat it as a toxicology emergency.
sourceBasis: American College of Medical Toxicology principles
